Department of Customs-Salaries, including R. R. Farrow at $2,150, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $45,000.

['My intention is to bring down all the details, and we will let the item stand.
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of the Minister of Finance, House adjourned at 11.30 p.m.', '

Tuesday, March 24, 1903.']

I ask leave to strike out all the words after ' salaries ' in the item. There has been a mistake in the preparation of the items and the accountant's salary of $2,150 has not been included so that I will have to bring in a supplementary estimate for his salary.
speakername: The MINISTER OP CUSTOMS (Hon. Wm. Paterson).

speechtext: I wish to make some observations on the frequency with which

the words ' notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act ' occur in these estimates.
I find that out of twenty-five items these words appear in eighteen. Now, the Civil Service Act was passed for the good purpose of regulating the qualifications of those who enter the service, and providing that they should have a fair remuneration which would be increased from year to year. I can understand that in the application of such a law there necessarily would be some rare exception. But these exceptions are growing greater and greater every year until in fact the exceptions have now become the rule. Surely it would be more creditable to the government to repeal the Civil Service Act completely or to amend it, rather than they should go on constantly violating it. It has become almost a scandal that there are so many flagrant violations of this Act by the government.

I would point out to the member for Grey (Mr. Sproule) that there are thirty-four officers included in this item, and the words 1 notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act ' would only apply to Mr. Farrow, the accountant.

I know that, but we are entitled to some better explanation from the government. Year after year we get some flippant answer when we inquire about this, until it has come to be that the Civil Service Act is almost entirely disregarded by the government.

We do not agree with the hon. gentleman that there is any abuse existing. We believe that the Civil Service Act serves a good purpose, but there are exceptional cases that can only be dealt with in an exceptional manner. The hon. gentleman says that out of twenty-five items, in eighteen of them these words occur. That may be correct, but let me point out that in the Department of Militia there are thirty-three officials and the words only apply to one out of that number. Is there any abuse in that ? In the Department of the Secretary of State there are twenty-six officials and the words apply to one official only. In the Department of Printing and Stationery there are twenty-seven officials and only one exception made, while in the Department of the Interior there are ninety-six officials and only two exceptions made. The hon. gentleman will see that there are not numerous exceptions, and even if there should be these words in connection with the items of every department of the government it would not follow that there was an abuse. It should only mean, and I hope it does only mean, that in one or two exceptional cases in a department these words are put in for reasons which of course must be explained to the House. I do not think there is any abuse : I do not think there is any reason to repeal

the Civil Service Act. In ninety-five per cent of the cases the general rules of the Act remain, and it is only to a small number in proportion to the total number of civil servants to which these words apply.
The Minister of Finance will admit that these words occur ten times more frequently in the estimates now than they did formerly.
I do not think so.

I have not made a precise count but I believe I am within the mark when I say so. If the civil service could be managed formerly within the four corners of the Act, why are the exceptions so numerous now ? Look at every department of the government in these estimates and you will see that some civil servant gets an increase " notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act." That certainly leaves the impression that either the Act place, it was intended to prevent him getting outside of the Act more and more every year. All the conditions were considered when the Act was passed. It started the civil servant at a fair salary, gave him a reasonable increase from year to year until he reached the maximum of his class, and then provided for promotion. Every thing reasonable is provided in the law and the constant violation of it is without excuse. The Act, in the first place, was intended to provide that the qualification of the civil servant should be such as to ensure his being a good and useful officer. In the second place, it was intended to prevent him getting salaries from two or three sources, because it had been found in many cases that the salary voted in the estimates was no indication of the whole amount an officer was paid. To prevent abuse in this respect the Act provided that his whole salary must be shown in the vote ; and where a rare exception occurred, as in the case of a civil servant who, from technical knowledge or special qualifications, would be required to do some work outside of the department to which he belonged, then something additional might be paid to him by saying ' notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act; ' but these exceptions were intended to be very few. Now they are becoming very many, and a great abuse is growing up, showing that the Act is not fulfilling the expectations of the House, and the government should either amend it or repeal it.

As my hon. friend has referred to the Department of Justice, I may state that I had in my department Mr. Blackadar, clerk of records, who received the maximum of his class. SI,400. The minimum salary of a junior second-class clerk is $000, but by paying $800 I can get all the duties performed for which Mr. Blackadar was paid $1,400. All 11
that my hon. friend points out is perfectly true, but providing the House is informed of what we are doing and the House exercises control over it, no very great harm can come to the service.

I need not remind the hon. gentleman of what occurred in the Department of Militia. The man who became a defaulter was brought in without having the qualifications which the Act called for, and we know what the result has been, though I do not attribute it exactly to the Act. But it shows the necessity of keeping within the Act, and if it is necessary to depart from it in special cases, let us provide for them by amendment to the Act and not by constantly setting it aside.

I notice that there is to be a new assistant commissioner, a new chief clerk, and two more junior clerks. Who is to be the new assistant commissioner, what is the necessity for his appointment, and what is the necessity for another chief clerk ?

The increase in the item now under discussion is $3,310, which will be increased to $5,400 when I bring down the suiiplementary vote for Mr. Farrow's salary. Of this increase, $2,800 is for the assistant commissioner. I think it will be apparent to hon. gentlemen why this appointment is made if they consider how greatly the work of the department has increased. In years gone by we had an assistant commissioner, who I think was Mr. Watters. After he left, the office was not continued, but I have felt that it was only due to the proper working of the department and in the public interest that we should have an assistant commissioner. The chief clerk referred to is Mr. Bremner, who gets the statutory increase of $30. Then, the hon. gentleman asks about the eight first-class clerks. One of these, Mr. Watson, it is proposed to raise from a second class clerkship to a first class.
What salary is he receiving now ?

$1,400. He will receive $1,800. He has shown special aptitude in taking supervision of the statistical department, which, as the hon. gentleman knows, was a comparatively small branch of the service in the city of Ottawa, but which has become large owing to the work which was previously done at the ports being now, done at headquarters. This has enabled us to get out our trade reports monthly. Then, Mr. Morin, a first-class clerk, is to be promoted to a chief clerkship, but as his salary is at the maximum, $1,800, it will remain the same.

Is Mr. Watson the senior clerk ?

The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS! No.
Will the hon. gentleman state what clerks he goes over that are his seniors ?

Mr. Watson goes to $1,400. He has $1,150 now. There is another clerk getting $1,150, two getting $1,200, one $1,250, three getting $1,400 and one $1,350. If you go by promotion, of course there are gentlemen getting larger salaries than he, but he is recognized as having peculiar fitness for the position. He has taken charge in a larger measure of that department, and it does not seem right that a gentleman who is really supervising those who are getting higher salaries should not have a salary somewhat befitting the position.
Does the Act allow you, where a party is not at the maximum of his class, to put him in another class where there is a vacancy ?
I think so.
The hon. gentleman hasj not told us yet who is to be the assistant commissioner.
I have a gentleman in my mind whom I thought of recommending to iny) colleagues. He is at present in the service.
Is he a chief clerk ?
No, his name is Mr. Bain.

The Minister of Customs has told the committee that the necessity arises from the increase in the work, but that is no explanation. The volume of the work may greatly increase without creating any necessity for an office of that kind. The increase is simply in clerical work which any clerk of ordinary capacity can do. Unless the hon. gentleman is prepared to show that the character of the work has been changed and that the change necessitates the appointment of an officer of that kind, he is without any excuse for fastening another officer on the public service. It would be much better to increase the salaries of those already engaged and who are doing clerical work. The position of commissioner is one of pure supervision, and his responsibility is very considerable. The commissioner or deputy head must be a man of ability and training and should be well paid. But the hon. gentleman now proposes to fasten another officer on the department on the plea that when Mr. Watters was there, there were two commissioners, or rather a commissioner and an assistant commissioner. But in the days when the hon. gentleman was filled with economy, he told the House that he had dispensed with Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
an assistant) commissioner because such an officer was not needed. Now, however, he says that an assistant commissioner is necessary because the volume of work has increased. But I do not think that excuse can be accepted. An increase in the mere volume of the work would not necessitate the appointment of an assistant commissioner, but only an increase in the character of the work to be done by ordinary clerks.

I should be very glad indeed to give the details concerning the work if I could, but I would ask) the committee to consider whether, on the face of it, they cannot see that when the business has increased to the extent it has, we must expect to get a little additional help. We have not increased the staff very much. I must give my predecessor's the credit which I gave them when criticising their administration from the opposition benches. It was generally recognized that the department was economically managed both by Sir Mackenzie Bowell and by Mr. Wallace who succeeded him, and when we consider that the trade in six months now Is equal to what it was in the twelve months when we took office, when we consider that the number of entries has nearly doubled, and that there are more ports, and a larger transit trade and more business altogether, I think the House will agree with me that the commissioner ought to be in the position of occasionally being able to leave his office and visit the principal ports and keep in touch with what is being done. If I had the hon. gentleman in my department and could show him the increase in the work, I think he would be satisfied.

The hon. gentleman gives us as one reason that there has been a large increase in the number of entries and in the volume of business. But surely he does not pretend to say that the commissioner makes a single entry or touches a pen in connection with that part of the work to which the hon. minister refers. The hon. gentleman might just as well ask for an increase in his own salary because of the increased work in his department. The cases are precisely parallel. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman thinks he should have an increase or not, but I can say that there is no more reason for the appointment of an assistant commissioner than there would be for increasing the hon. gentleman's salary. The increased volume of business does not entail on the minister more work than he had to attend to when he first took office, although I will admit his responsibility must have increased. I admit the responsibility; but the work to be done by reason of the increased business in the department is, 99 per cent, I venture to say, a class of work that could be done by any efficient clerk. The hon. gentleman knows the growing tendency under our sys-

tem-and I am not going to impute the blame to this government any more than to any former government-to fasten upon the public service men who have no sound claim to the positions to which they are appointed. No man has any claim in himself to be employed in the public service-the public interest is the only ground on which such appointments should be made. The hon. gentleman, I am sure, is quite convinced that be has a very worthy gentleman, whom he wishes to place there. During the time 1 have had the honour of a seat in this House, I have never once attached the salary received by an official. My belief is that Canada must first secure good service, and Canada has no more right to demand good service at less than its worth than any individual employer has. Therefore, we are bound to give fair remuneration to the men who are absolutely necessary. But we only minimize the chances of proper advance on the part of the men of merit, if we chuck into the service men who are not needed, I venture the opinion that the hon. minister has not made out a case to justify the change he proposes.

I do not think there is any class of people in the Dominion that are so poorly paid as the officials in the departments of the government. We speak of the prosperity of the Dominion, but we are apt to forget that prosperity increases the expense of living, so that this prosperity has not been of much advantage to these officials. I think it very desirable that the Minister of Customs should be able to leave his office oftener than he does to visit the principal ports of the country and see how the work is conducted there. And if the minister himself cannot always make those visits I think the commissioner of customs should be sent around from time to time to examine the different ports. When I was collector of customs, a position I occupied for fourteen years till my friends opposite thought it not in their interests that I should be there any longer, the Minister of Customs, Sir Mackenzie Bowell, used to visit our port and spend days and days there. I speak with some knowledge when I say it is very desirable that either the Minister of Customs or his commissioner should visit the most important ports and see how the work of the department in those ports is carried on. The men who grow up in the different departments of the public service have their minds run into one groove, so that they become unfit for any other positions than those they occupy. They have not the slightest hope of ever being profited by anything until Providence shall take them away to a better country.

What are the initials of the Mr. Watson whom the hon. minister proposes to raise ?
11*
His name is John Archibald Watson. He was appointed in the summer of 1891.
Was he appointed as a second class clerk ?
He is in the second class clerk list.
Was he originally ?
I think he has been in the second class ever since I came into the department.

When the hon. minister, in presenting his estimates, has to announce an important change like this- I am not saying he is not perfectly justified in making it-altering the theoretical organization of his department, he ought to be prepared to give the reasons for the change. I notice, from the statement the hon. gentleman gives us, that the gentleman whom he intends to appoint assistant commissioner-though he may be deserving of the position-only entered the service in 1896. He is now, I think, a first class clerk receiving a salary of $1,500 a year with an allowance as private secretary. The hon. minister must consider the demoralization of the whole staff when he takes a man, who only entered the service in 1896, appoints him a first class clerk and then promotes him over the heads of even the chief clerks and makes him assistant commissioner. There must be some strong reason given to justify such a course. We want something more than the mere bald statement that there is an increase in the work of the department. The hon. gentleman should, as I have said, be ready to give us reasons for this change in the theoretical organization of his department and he should be able also to tell us what are the special qualifications of this gentleman who is to be thus put over the heads of others and appointed assistant commissioner.

The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has mentioned one point which removes an objection by the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy). That hon. gentleman seemed to think we were bringing a new man into the service. That is not the case-this is the promotion of a man who has been six or seven years in the service.
I did not raise that objection and did not inquire as to that point. I objected to the nature of the hon. gentleman's (Hon. Mr. Paterson's) explanation, whomever it might apply to.

I thought the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) spoke of our wishing to bring some one into the service. But it seems I was wrong as to what the hon. gentleman said. I have already explained that I wished to ease the

work upon tlie commissioner so that he may have liberty to leave his office and visit the principal ports, and, when he is in the office I wish him to have an assistant whom he may consult. It is desirable, also, to have one who can take the commissioner's place when he is absent. At present, a chief clerk must be called in to fill the place. As to promoting a man over the heads of others the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has administered a department and he knows that it is quite possible that a man may be found who, though not so long in the service as others, has developed a perculiar fitness to fill a certain position. And, when he found such a man, I am sure he did not hesitate to give him the position. The gentleman I have mentioned, who is to receive this appointment if the House pass the salary and my colleagues approve, is not excelled by any one in the service in his grasp of the business or otherwise better fitted for the position. I think that any one who knows him will agree as to his qualifications. And, reverting to the question of promotion over the heads of others, the hon. gentleman must remember that the commissioner of customs, of whom I desire to speak in the highest terms and whom I regard as one of the most faithful officers in the service, was not in the civil service at all, but came from outside and was appointed at the very head of the department. I am bound to say that experience has justified the selection of that gentleman. The work has been well done indeed. The work that that commissioner renders is greater than hon. gentlemen opposite, not acquainted with it as they are expected to be, have any idea of. Now with reference to the remark of the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) who complains that the commissioner has not more work. He seems to think that he sits in his office and that all he has to do is to say to a certain clerk, Do this, and to another one, do that. Why, these clerks have to consult with him in reference to the business, correspondence has to be conducted, and letters written. And though he does not do merely clerical work himself, he has to be consulted with regard to it, and any one who visits his office, I venture to say, will find that he is a very busy man. Therefore, I desire an assistant commissioner, in order to relieve him somewhat of his too onerous duties, and who will take his place when it is necessary for him, in the public interest, to visit some of the larger ports and transshipping points, as I think he should do much oftener. I need not say more. I chink if the hon. gentleman was administering the department he would be of the same nind as myself. I need not go into further details. I state the broad fact that the work has increased to such an extent that help is needed, and I am asking for a first-class clerk. The hon. gentleman complains that he is to be put over the heads of others.

I grant you that this Mr. Watson we propose to raise is going over some others ; but in the judgment of the commissioner and of myself he has special aptitude for the position he is filling at present, greater than some others that are there, and for that reason I am asking the committee to grant an additional salary so that he may take his rank as a first-class clerk. It seems only fair and right, since he is in a position like that, supervising other first-class clerks, that he should not be paid a salary inferior to that which they get.

I think we should have some other items of information before this vote is passed. I see that the Civil Service Act provides that
The Governor in Council shall from tune to time determine the number of officers, chief clerks, clerks, messengers and other employes that are required for the working of the several departments in each division of the civil service. '
They should determine that from time to time. Have the Governor in Council determined that in that department another chief clerk is necessary ? Because, if not, it is done in violation of the Act.
Yes, and there will have to be an amendment to the Customs Act passed in the House before this office is created, and it will come, of course, by consent of the government.

It seems to me you are starting at the wrong end of the business. You first vote the salary, and then you go to the Governor in Council to set you right. According to my understanding of the law, the Governor in Council first have to consider whether the work there necessitates an additional chief clerk. And the Act provides that after that is done the salary for the additional chief clerk can be voted.
All appointments to the civil service shall he during pleasure, and no person shall he appointed or promoted to any place below that of a deputy head unless he has passed the requisite examination and served the probationary term hereinafter mentioned.
I notice that in most of these cases there is no satisfactory evidence that they have served their probationary term in one class to entitle them to be moved into another, and it requires an Order in Council to move them in violation of the Civil Service Act.
A first-class clerkship shall only be created by Order in Council.
That Order in Council has not passed, and we are providing a salary for a chief clerkship before we know that one is needed, before the Governor in Council have exercised their judgment as to whether one is needed or not. It seems to me the hon. gentleman is going to work entirely in the wrong way.

A chief clerkship in any department shall only be created by Order in Council, passed after the deputy head has reported that such an officer is necessary for the proper performance of the public business in 1he department, stating the reasons on which ho has arrived at that conclusion.
Then the concurrence of the head of the department is required. Then it is provided that a first-class clerkship should only be created by Order in Council, and a second-class clerkship also by Order in Council. But in every one of these instances the first or theoretical part, as the hon. member for Lanark says, must be determined by Order in Council according as the need of the service requires these additional clerks ; and that is done after careful examination, and after recommendation by the head of the branch, sanctioned by the Deputy Minister and by the minister himself. But here the first thing we do is to vote the salary upon the statement of the minister that the work is increasing there. I think his course is radically wrong.
The salary of a clerk on appointment or promotion to any class shall begin at the minimum of such class.
In nearly every instance we are violating that provision of the Act. They do not commence at the minimum, and they start the salary above the minimum. In other respects also we are violating the Act, because we take clerks from one class and promote them to another before they have reached the maximum of that class.
No salary shall be paid to any member of the civil service whose appointment or promotion, or whose increase of salary after the *first day of July, 1882, has not been made in the manner provided in the Civil Service, Act in force at the time of such appointment, promotion or increase.
In every one of these instances we are violating the law, in other words, we are voting these sums outside the Act entirely, we do so saying ' Notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act.' Therefore I say I was justified in taking strong exception to the abuse that has crept into the departments.
But you must have the provision made before the Order in Council is formally passed.
No.
Yes, you cannot appoint a person to that position with a salary unless the House has sanctioned the grant.

The minister is entirely wrong. His first duty is to change the theoretical organization of his department on recommendation of the deputy head, and get an Order in Council, assigning reasons for it. Then there is a reason for parliament voting the salary. You cannot appoint a party to a position until the salary
is voted, or at least if you do appoint him, you cannot pay him the salary until it is voted. The first duty of the minister is to get his deputy head to concur with him as to the necessity of a change in the theoretical organization of his department, then get the approbation of his colleagues in council, and the sanction of the Governor. When he has got that, he comes here and asks us to vote the salary. Then when the minister says that the deputy head did not pass the examination
I did not say that.
That he was appointed to the position without examination, or without passing through the lower grades.
No, not examination.

Well, he was appointed to the position without passing through any lower grade to the deputy head of the department and the hon. minister knows that the Civil Service Act does not apply to the deputy head at all.
It does not apply to the deputy head.

And there are several other offices that are exempted and the hon. minister must remember-it was stated again aud again-the reasons why. There must be some offices in the country at the disposal of the government of the day as a reward for political services and as a reward to men of ability in the House for services to their country. Among them are the deputy headships of the departments, the postmasterships iu the different towns and cities and the eollectorships of customs in the different towns and cities. The justification that he has given is no justification at all because the reason does not apply in this case. He does not come to the House and tell us that lie' has the approval of the Governor in Council for a change in the theoretical organization of the department as the Civil Service Act requires. He should be prepared with all these reasons to give to the Committee and particularly to tell why it is that the theoretical organization of his department is changed and whether it is changed with the approbation of the deputy head of the department.

When the hon. gentleman says that I have not the sanction of the Governor in Council for this act he is mistaken. Council agreed to this ; it would not have been in the estimates if they had not agreed to it. It is the salary that is being asked for. This officer cannot be appointed until the salary is provided for and he cannot be appointed until an Order in Council lias passed appointing him ; but. I am asking meanwhile

whether the committee will sanction the payment of a salary to a person to be appointed to the office who must be appointed, of course, by the Governor in Council, and who will be.

The hon. minister is trying to impose upon the Committee and upon me. He says that he has the sanction of the Governor in Council for the estimates brought down and therefore that he has his sanction for the change in the theoretical organization of his department. But, the Civil Service Act requires that the deputy head of the department shall approve of the theoretical organization and that there shall be an Order in Council passed approving of it. Does the hon. minister say that anything of that kind is done and does he say that because he has the consent of the Governor in Council to the bringing down of his estimates and presenting them before the House he has the approval of the Governor in Council for this appointment ?
Contingencies, including $1,750, which may he paid notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $10,355.

I beg to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) to the fact that the contingencies are to be paid notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act. I understood the hon. minister to say that the whole of the contingencies are intended to be paid in that manner.
No, I did not express any opinion. My hon. friends must explain that for themselves I did not say that.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I understood that the hon. minister said, when I mentioned contingencies, that it was not intended to apply to the Civil Service Act.
I certainly did not say anything of the kind. If I said that I was mistaken.
Well then I mistook what the hon. minister said, but he must see that the vote for contingencies applies to everything under that head and that the Civil Service Act does not apply.

No, the explanation is this :	There is an amount
voted for contingencies and in that amount is included $1,750.
Why do you not put it so in your estimates ?
I think it is so stated.
Not at all ; it is nothing of the kind. Put it plainly.

I do not know how the hon. gentleman would word Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
it. Contingencies, including $1,750, which may be paid notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act.
There is a comma after $1,750.
It is only the $1,750 to which the Act does not apply.
Not at all.
If the comma is struck out that is the way it reads.

Strike out the comma and it may be so. Contingencies, $1,750, which may be paid notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act-if that does not apply to the whole of the contingencies I know nothing about the English language or construction of it.
That is not intended.
Well then, put it in the form in which it is intended.
$1,750 is the amount out of the contingencies that may be paid notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act.
Well then, change it so as to make it clear.
Strike out the comma ; strike out the comma.

Yes, strike out the comma. I have explained before that the way in which this $1,750 came into the estimates was that a first-class clerk who had been drawing $1,750 a year became ill. He took a trip for his health, I think, to the North-west and, unfortunately, on his way, he died. Between the passing of the original and supplementary estimates this took place. When we came to the sup-plementaries I dropped the vote for a first-class clerk of $1,750 and took a vote for that amount, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act. I then got two men for the $1,750 that the one man had got before and the money is being used in that way. It has passed now for two or three years in that way.

Let me suggest this amendment :	Contingencies, of which
$1,750 may be paid notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act.
I accept that; perhaps it is better.
The hon. minister did not explain who these two second-class clerks were. Have they been taken out of those who have been temporary clerks in the department ?

The two second-class clerks are in the service now,

Mr. Schofield, who has been there for six years Is getting $600 a year and Wm. Wall, who has been in the department for five years is getting $550. The first of these was paid out of the Board of Customs vote- that is the outside vote. The salary of the other has been paid out of contingencies, the item under consideration now. Instead of one being paid out of the Board of Customs vote and the other out of contingencies they become second-class clerks and their salaries are provided for in another item.
I see that the contingencies stand at the same amount notwithstanding that this clerk was paid out of contingencies formerly.

Yes, I leave the contingencies at the same amount because I am afraid we will have to use the extra amount. But, the total, as the hon. gentleman will see, of the advance for the department of contingencies and salaries combined is $5,460. I beg to move that this item be amended so as to read : ' Contingencies of which $1,750 may be paid notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act.'
Item as amended, agreed to.

The small increase was on the recommendation of the deputy ; there is no change in the staff, and notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act.

None whatever; it is going along in peace and harmony.
Department of Railways and Canals-Salaries, including J. W. Pugsley at S1,S00, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $45,950 ; contingencies, $8,000.

The net increase in the vote this year over last year is $800. That is made out in this way : We hn ve allowed the usual statutory increases, which amount to $750. We have increased Mr. Pugsley's salary $100 and we have promoted Mr. Little, Mr. Bell, and Mr. Wright-Mr. Little from a second class clerk to a first class clerk. Mr. Little was appointed in the service in 1881 as a third class clerk; promoted to a second class clerk in 1900. He has been performing the duties in the accountant's branch previously done by the assistant accountant. 1-Ie is a faithful and industrious officer and we have promoted him to the first class. We have promoted Mr. Bell from a junior second class to a second class clerk, and we have promoted Mr. J. P. Wright from
a junior second class clerk to a second class clerk. These three cases involve an increase over the salaries which they now receive of $550. We make provisions for two junior second class clerks which will add $1,200. The total increase caused by the staututory increase and by the additions to the salaries and promotions which I have mentioned will total $2,600. We have one first class clerk less whose salary was $1,800, leaving a net result of $800 as an addition to the appropriation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Had these clerks reached the maximum of their class in each case before you promoted them ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: When did Mr. Pugsley come into the service and why do you have to say ' notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act ' ?

Mr. Pugsley entered the service in 1S80; he was appointed third class clerk in 1883; he became a second class clerk in 1890; he was promoted first class clerk in 1896; he has been clerk of the Committee of the Privy Council since February, 1896. The increase will make his salary $1,800.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the minister looks at the estimates he will see that he is voting the same number of first class clerks as there were last year. There must be some mistake if you have one first class clerk less now. Your estimates are wrongly printed as presented to the House.
We are only asking for the amount of money that we require.

There are only ten now including Mr. Pugsley.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister stated very definitely a little while ago that he had dropped one first-class clerk-in other words, that he had one less now than he had last year. I ask the minister to tell us definitely how many he had last year and how many he has this year.
Which one did you drop?
I cannot tell you. My memorandum does not show.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understand that the minister is making some additional junior clerkships and one additional first-class clerkship. Did he first get the consent of council to this increase, as the Act provides ?
Yes, the Governor in Council undoubtedly assented to the appropriation being asked for the increase. That is all that has been done.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then the hon. minister Is doing in his department what has been done in the Customs Department-commencing at the wrong end. The Act provides that the Governor in Council shall first determine how many clerks are required for each department.
They determined on that when they agreed to the estimates.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is not complying with the Act at ail. They must first provide for the number in the different classes; and after that the salaries are voted, when they are recommended by the head of the department. But it appears this has not been done in the department of the Minister of Railways nor in the department of the Minister of Customs, and I presume that the same practice has been followed throughout the various departments. Therefore the Civil Service Act has been entirely ignored by the government.

I think my hon. friend's remarks are based upon a misconception. His argument is that you must first create the clerkship before you come to the House for a vote. Sly hon. friend is mistaken. The Civil Service Act distinctly declares the reverse. Section 15 provides that a chief clerkship in any department shall only be created by Order in Council passed after the report of the deputy, after the concurrence of the head of the department in such report, and after the salary has been voted by parliament. These various conditions must first be complied with before the Governor in Council creates an additional clerkship. The same rule is carried down to a first-class clerkship. Section 17 provides that a first-class clerkship can only be created by an Order in Council passed on a report of the deputy head, concurred in by the head of the department, setting forth the reasons for creating the office, and after the salary has been voted by parliament. The same condition applies to a second-class clerkship. In each of these cases before the Governor in Council can grant an additional clerkship, parliament must first have provided the money. The first step is to get the appropriation from parliament.
That is not the provision of the Act to which I refer.
I take this from the Act as published in the civil service list, dated 1902, and which contains all the amendments.

I refer to section 6 :
The Governor in Council shall, from time to time determine the number of officers, chief clerks, clerks, messengers and other employees required for the working of the several departments in each division of the ci7il service.
What I complain of is that the Governor in Council have not brought their judgment to bear on this at all. The minister at the head of the department has simply found it necessary to put on another mau, and asks us to provide for the salary before the| Governor in Council have decided whether the requirements of the work call for another man.
The Governor in Council can only consider the matter after parliament has voted the money. It can do nothing with regard to creating offices until the appropriation is voted.
How can you determine how much money you want before determining what number of clerks you require ? You. must do that before asking us to vote the money.

The House is entitled to have the opinion of the Cabinet before any proposition is submitted to it to change the organization of any department. We are entitled to have first the recommendation to the minister at the head of the department made by the deputy head. That recommendation ought to be on record. Then the matter should be brought before the Governor in Council and considered, and it is only on the approval of the! Governor in Council that the minister at the head of the department has a right to ask parliament to vote the money. This is not a mere matter of form. We are entitled to have the guarantee and pledge of the Governor in Council that the necessity exists for the change. More than that, until the Governor in Council has determined that there is a necessity for an increase, the minister at the head of the department cannot estimate what amount of money he will require. It is a very serious neglect of the primary conditions upon which we are called upon to vote the estimates that, not in one department alone, but in all the departments, this very important provision of the Civil Service Act is ignored.

What I said is further substantiated by the subsection 2 of section 6 :
If the number of employees then attached to any department In either division is greater than the number allowed to the department as herein provided, the Governor in Council shall name the persons to fill the several offices ; and the remainder shall bo supernumerary clerk3 without being eligible for increase of salary, of that class respectively in which they rank, and shall so remain until promoted in (he manner herein provided or until severed from the service.

Assuming the hon. gentleman to be right in his interpretation of the Civil Service Act, it would have no application to the present case. Taking it for granted that before the change of government, such subjects had been dealt with precisely as the hon. gentleman says they should have been, the number of employees authorized by the Governor in Council was 28. After I came into the department two vacancies occurred, and these were not filled, so that we have had but 26 permanent employees in the department instead of 28. Therefore, according to the interpretation of the hon. gentleman, since the Governor in Council decided that 28 permanent clerks were necessary for the proper organization of the department, and since there are now only 26 there, we have the right to ask for the appointment of the other two, without again going before the Governor in Council.
speakername: The MINISTER OE RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

I promote and leave a junior second-class clerkship vacant.

The hon. minister does not think it is, necessary for the Governor in Council to exercise his judgment so long as he keeps below the number which the Governor in Council [DOT]authorizes.

I do not interpret the Act as the hon. gentleman does. I think that the view stated by the Minister of Finance is the correct one. But, without assuming that all these performances would have to be gone through with any ordinary case it
is not necessary in the present case, for the reason that, what they may reasonably have for the purposes of work of the department will not be exceeded by the votes I am now asking for.

make. I want $45,950 on account of salaries, exactly as stated in the estimates.

Contingencies, including L. Charbcraneau at $500, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $12,000.

I was asking the hon. minister if it was intended to do away with the observatory at Toronto.

I do not think this interferes at all with the observatory at Toronto. This is under the direction of the Interior Department and it has been in existence in Ottawa for a great many years. There will, of course, be a great improvement in the service, in the building, accommodation and equipment. But, it does not interfere with the observatory at Toronto. The observatory at Toronto. I think, is in connection with the Marine Deparment and it serves a different purpose altogether.
As the estimates we are now passing are for the year ending June, 1904, why not put the whole amount in ?

I understand my hon. friend's point now. The foundation of this work is completed Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
and the chief architect estimates that this $45,000 is all the contractor will earn during the time for which we take this vote. The building is not expected to be completed until next season, though the contract requires it to be completed on the 25th June. Yes.

* Can the hon. minister give any information as to what astronomer is to be in charge and whether there is any person supervising the work who is possessed of the technical knowledge necessary to provide a suitable structure for the purpose ?

This is not connected with the Public Works Department, but as I happen to know, I do not object to giving the information. Mr. King is a gentleman that I believe the House has a great deal of confidence in and he is at the head of this work. There is no contemplated change in the staff, so far as my information goes. The staff is perfectly satisfactory and from the reports I have seen it has received a great deal of praise from some of the older countries that spend a great many thousand dollars on this service.
