speechtext:
I know him very well.
Ottawa-Branch of Royal Mint, $50,000.
Would the hon. minister explain how that matter stands ?

I am afraid it is standing still. It was decided by the department under my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte), to place the building on the government property near the Printing Bureau. The Militia Department which has control of that property raised some objections, and I believe that information was received from the authorities in England, that in building a mint for the reception of minting plant you require to have a very solid and exceedingly level surface. Therefore some difficulty was found, outside of the objection of the Militia De-

partment, towards occupying the site chosen. That has occasioned delay. I hope that delay will not be much longer. I think that on the same property, probably on the other side, we will be able to find ground enough to carry out the plan prepared by the department when my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) was minister. The same plan is in every way satisfactory if we had a suitable site. I hope to have a report to-day, but at all events I will have it in a short time and I think the chief architect will report that we can have a level site on the other side.
Do I understand that it will be the same site ?
No, ou the other side.
When I left office these objections had not been raised.
I do not think so.
Why, it is on solid rock.

In order to get a level surface, there would be a good deal of cutting down necessary and much expense would have to be gone to, and it would not give an opportunity for driving around as laid down in the plan. When I went to the department I found that nothing had been done and I asked for a report. So far as I can say at present, if the other site is found satisfactory, it will be adopted.

I cannot understand where that other site is. I may say at once that when I left office no objection of the kind had been raised The bottom is rock and there can be no possible objection on the ground of solidity.
There has been an earthquake since.

The Minister of Finance and myself had agreed as to the site and I cannot for the life of me discover why the English authorities, who had approved of the plan when I left office, raised the objection since. I would like to have some more knowledge as to the nature of these objections because I cannot understand them at all. Indeed I do not know where the present site can be and perhaps it is only fair to ask that the item should stand until we have more information about it.

It is three years since this vote was first taken and when I went into the department I endeavoured to have the work go ahead. The country and parliament is committed to it and I believe it is an important work in the interest of the country. Of course if the House wishes to renew this vote I shall submit the plan.

The reason why the work did not go on so rapidly as it will perhaps go on now, is that the Minister of Finance asked me to delay until he returned from England. That is the reason why the contract was not awarded but as to the site it was decided upon when I left office. I am sure the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr Sutherland) does not accuse me of losing time. The plans were prepared, they had to be sent to England to be approved of, and the Minister of Finance asked me before his last trip to England not to give the contract before he came back.

There seems to be a contradiction in the statement by the minister. First the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) was told that there had been a change in the site, and it would now appear that there has been no change in the site.

My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) is correct in what he says. He had commenced proceedings with the view of building the mint on Nepean Point, close to the Printing Bureau, and he had gone so far as to call for tenders. He was good enough to make a delay until I could return from England, and on or about that time objections were made by the Militia Department, and perhaps from other sources as to the suitability of the site, and it was proposed to look for a new site. I am aware of the site which my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) has in his mind, but as it includes some private land, perhaps we would not be wise in indicating at present where that land is until it is under option. I do not think any business man would think it wise to announce that we were going to buy a certain piece of property until we had that property under option.
Hear, hear.

When I left office the government had chosen a site on government ground. I want to emphasize that fact. Of course if the minister tells me that he has good ground for asking that the item should go through I will make no more objection.
Might I ask the Minister of Militia and Defence what are his objections to the site in question. Of course, if it is against the public interest, I do not wish him to answer.

I have no objection to say that after the plans were matured it was found that very much more ground would be required for the buildings than was at first supposed, and that it might interfere with the use of that ground for military purposes in future. If for instance there should ever be a military depot at Ottawa it might be a convenient site for such a building. I had a careful report made upon the matter by

the then General Officer Commanding and I addressed a letter to the Minister of Finance suggesting that there should be delay until the whole question could be considered.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
This being the third time that this vote has been placed in the estimates for a royal mint at Ottawa, it seems to me that I should now ask the Minister of Public Works, if the government intends building the mint this year. If I am correctly informed the Minister of Finance is not in favour of building a mint because he says that the mint will be an absolute loss to Canada.
Some bon. MEMBERS. Oh.
The Minister of Finance is reported as having so stated. I wonder if I am correct or not in that.
I wonder if my hon. friend will give me the source of his information.
Yes I will.
In the earlier stages there was some debate about the advisability of our having a mint but for several years it has been the policy of both sides of the House that a mint should be built.

Well, I will read it. On the 15th of May, 1899, Mr. Fielding made a speech in the House of Commons against the establishment of a mint in Canada. His speech will be found in ' Hansard ' for 1899, pages 3112 and 3113. Mr. Fielding said :
I am well within the mark when I say that a well equipped mint would turn out m one month all the copper and silver coins required in Canada in the whole year so that we would have an establishment with one mouth's work, and eleven months' idleness.
Were we to adopt this policy we would lose a considerable part of the profit we are now enjoying-that is the profit out of the coinage.
Were we to convert all our gold into coin we* would find that we had no use for it.
There is no profit in the minting of gold.
Not only is there no profit, but there would be absolute loss.
It would be a waste of money to have a Canadian mint.
Iu the face of that, I think it is my duty, as one of the representatives of the city of Ottawa, to ask the Minister of Public Works if it is the intention of the government to establish a mint in Ottawa or merely to keep this vote dangling before the eyes of the electors from year to year ?

When the hon. gentleman stated that he had been informed by somebody that the Minister of Finance had opposed this mint vote, he was mistaken, because he had not been informed, but was reading from an old debate dealing with the question of a mint under entirely different conditions from those which

exist to-day. We are not proposing to establish a mint in the manner which was then under debate, but a branch of the royal mint of England, which will mint not only the coinage of Canada, but also the sovereign of the British Empire from Canadian gold, am entirely different proposition. So that my hon. friend is reading from an old story, under conditions which have vastly changed, and his zeal on behalf of his constituents has certainly not been so great as it ought to be when he is giving a turn to my remarks entirely unwarranted by the experience of the past three years.
I am certainly indebted to the hon. Minister of Finance for the information he has1 given; but I did not misquote him.
I did not say the hon. gentleman did.

My information is correct. The statement was made by the hon. gentleman, and he never contradicted it. If there was no profit in minting gold three years ago, where do you expect to get the profit now ? I merely want to know, on behalf of my constituents, whether it is the intention of the government to establish this mint or not, or whether they intend to keep this $50,000 vote dangling before the electors until the next election comes around?
The hon. gentleman says he did not misquote me. I do not accuse him of misquoting me. He is reading from a newspaper report of what occurred three years ago.
No, I ana reading from ' Hansard.'

Well, it is not my practice to delve into those old records unless I have some special reason; but my recollection is that I stated then that if we could arrange to establish a branch of the royal mint, and not simply a mint for Canadian currency, that might be worth while. When he saysi he is obliged to me for the information I have given, he need not thank me, because I did not give him any information that has not been before the House for a long time, and if the hon. gentlepaan has not discovered it until now, he is not as wide-awake a representative of the city of Ottawa as I had supposed he was.

I think the very fact that the item has been voted for three years is a very good reason for the hon. member for Ottawa asking the question he has, especially in view of the information which we have now that the government has not even selected the site for the mint. I wish to ask what is the estimated cost of this mint.

A very full estimate has been made. It is

estimated that it will cost at least $275,000, or perhaps, when fully equipped, about $300,000. I may say to my hon. friend the member for Ottawa that since this policy was decided upon, no member of the government has had the slightest intention of delaying the work of putting up the building. So far as the Finance Minister is concerned, during the few weeks that I have been in the department, he has bothered me with regard to it, both in writing and personally, on several occasions. I am making every possible effort to have the work commenced, and I hope, if this vote meets the approval of the House, that when the supplementary estimates for the coming year are brought down, I shall be able to give full information as to the site, and as to what additional amount will be required in order to enable us to go on with the building during the year 1903-4. By that time we ought to be able to advertise for tenders and to know exactly when we can go on with the work.

The hon. Minister *of Finance has given a curious excuse for his change of opinion. Three years ago he held exactly the opinion stated by the hon. member for Ottawa. He has had the item in the estimates for three years, so that It must have been only this year that he has received the consent of the imperial authorities to establish a branch of the royal mint. Why did he ask for al vote two years ago, without having that consent, and when he held the opinion that the mint was entirely - useless ? It is only this year, as I understand, that he has received the authority of the imperial authorities, to do what he proposes to do.
Who said that ?
I understood that you said it.
I did not say anything of the sort.
The hon. minister, in answering the objections of my hon. friend from Ottawa, stated that when he made his statement three years ago he had a different opinion.
No, I did not.

And that because of the authority he has received from the imperial authorities, another state of affairs exists. When was it he got the authority ? Was it last year, or the year before ? It could not have been the year before, because it was then proposed not to build this mint in the city of Ottawa, but in Vancouver or somewhere else in British Columbia, for the purpose of minting the gold mined in the Yukon and keeping it in our *own country.

My hon. friend has the unhappy faculty of understanding a great many things that nobody says. I certainly did not say any of the things the hon. gentleman attributes to me. As to when the authority of the imperial government was obtained, when the Act of this parliament was passed to establish a mint, it was distinctly stated that it was to be established in Ottawa; it was never proposed to put it anywhere else. The whole matter was threshed out in this House at that time, and the Act passed two years ago was to establish not a purely Canadian mint, but a branch of the royal mint.

I may say that it was claimed during the election contest in the Yukon that if a supporter of the government were sent here, there would be a chance of having the mint established at Dawson. It was also stated in British Columbia when I was out there that it was desirable to have a mint at Vancouver, therefore it was necessary that the government should be supported in that quarter. Down here in| Ottawa, I presume the same thing was dangled before the people so as to show them it was very desirable the government should be sustained. Why, the party opposite have been making use of this question in various localities. Certainly some one has been deceiving the people, and the fact that we have been voting the money three or four sessions and not spending any part of it gives colour to the belief that the whole thing is kept open for political purposes.

I do not see how any one could pretend that the site for this building was to be elsewhere than in Ottawa. The grant was taken for a mint at Ottawa. The Act was passed for the establishment of a government mint at Ottawa, and no member of the government has ever proposed that it should be anywhere else than in Ottawa. All this political scheming exists only in the imagination of the hon. gentleman.
The fact that you are not spending the grant is sufficient to give rise to the suspicion that you are using this item as a bait for political support.
Suspicion ever haunts the guilty mind.

It took some time for the plans to be got ready as that kind of work is new here. After the plans were prepared they had to be sent to England, and we wrote, I do not know how many times, to get these plans back before we could get them. In England they do not do things so quickly as my hon. friend would like to see them done here. We lost a great deal of time before we could get the plans back. Tenders were asked for, but my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, who was going to England, thought it was better that

lie should consult personally with the imperial authorities before anything further was done, and that was why the contract was not awarded. I may be mistaken, but 1 am afraid that the choice of a new site will require the making of new plans. The plans were prepared for the site at Nepean Point, and no objection was then raised to that site. There was some talk about that piece of land being required for military purposes but we got over that difficulty, and tenders were called for.
When were tenders called for ?
About five months ago.

Had an agreement between the imperial authorities and the Canadian government been arrived at then ?
Hon. air. TARTE. Yes, we had full authority then, but the Minister of Finance was anxious to see the imperial authorities again. The arrangement for the site however was final, because I called for tenders and I am afraid that if a new site be chosen new plans will have to be prepared.

In connection with this item, there is another item of $200,000 which was formerly voted for the new geological museum at Ottawa. It was twice voted by this House but I do not see it in the estimates this session.
The ailNISTER OF FINANCE. It is in the estimates. In 1901 we passed the Act, entitled an Act respecting the Ottawa Branch of the Royal Mint. That Act, it is provided, may be cited as " The Ottawa aiint Act, 1901." How in the face of that anybody can say that the government at any time entertained the idea of putting the mint anywhere else, is something I cannot understand.

In view of the statement made by the ex-Minister of Public Works, that the consent of the imperial authorities had been obtained and tenders called fox-, why did the Minister of Finance ask for further delay until he could see the imperial authoi'ities.

My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) was calling for tenders during my absence and I suggested that the contract should not be awarded until my return. I desii'ed to consult the imperial authorities-not to obtain their consent, because that had been given-but about some matters of detail. I asked my hon. friend to be good enough to hold over the tenders until my return and he was kind enough to do so.
Did the hon. gentleman raise any question with reference to the foundation not being good, because the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sutherland) lays special stress upon the fact that the build-
ing would require a very solid foundation^ thereby implying that the site already selected was not sufficiently solid.

I did not say that. I may have said that the building required a solid foundation but the site referred to by my hon. friend is perfectly solid. It required however to be levelled and the surroundings levelled.

If I understand the objection, it was that the ground was not broad enough. As to that I am not prepared to say anything except that when I left office the ground had been found sufficiently large. Of course this is a very important building, and the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Public Works have a pei'fect right to choose a better site if one is to be found.
Is it possible for the hon. Minister of Public Works to tell us what pi'oportion of land belonging to individuals and what proportion belonging to the government will be taken for this site.
I cannot give that at pi'esent.
And how many thousand feet more would be requii'ed.
I shall get that information.
I see an item of $50,000 for the Victoria Museum, but surely that is not intended to replace the geological mu- [DOT] seum ?
We will reach that in a moment.

I asked why the $200,000 which was twice voted for the geological museum was dropped. Two years ago I was given to understand that plans had been prepared for a building which was to cost $1,000,000. Has the Department of Public Works any plans for this museum, for which $200,000 was voted two years ago ?
When were the $200,000 voted ?
In 1901-2, for a new geological museum at Ottawa, and that was estimated as one-fifth of the total cost.
That amount was voted, but when we found that it could not be spent we simply reduced it. There was no use voting a lai-ge amount in the estimates when it could not be spent ?
There were only $50,000 voted in 1901.

I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken. My present colleague (Mr. Belcourt) told me distinctly that he had the plan of this building at home in his own residence and the building was to cost | $1,000,000.
When was that ?
20th October, 1900. Are those plans still in the possession of the government ?
When was that ?
In 1900-on the 29th of October. I want to know if these plans are still in the possession of the government?

Sufficient has come out in this debate with regard to buying more land, to justify us in calling upon the government to lay before the country a plan for acquiring land in Ottawa for the purposes of government on a comprehensive scale. Every now and again a proposition is brought up to buy land here or to rent it there for the purposes of the government. The time has come when a large block of land should be acquired in Ottawa for government purposes. That land could be acquired for a reasonable price. It ought to be got now ; the government should cease this tinkering way of acquiring land here or there at heavy prices and against the public interest. There is opportunity for jobbery in every such deal.
I would like to ask the minister if it is the government's intention to locate this mint according to the plans now in the possession of the government ?

My information from the chief architect is that the plans are quite satisfactory. They have been approved by the British government. And I am perfectly frank in stating that, when I get this vote, if then my colleagues approve, the work will be gone on with as soon as possible.
Has the whole site or only part of the site been bought ? Of course, if I am indiscreet in asking that question, I shall not press it.

My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) and the House will see that it would be indiscreet of me-holding the views I do, and intending, as I do, to ask council and this House to endorse any action we may take-to answer that question now. I agree with my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) 12
that it is in the public interest that these important national buildings should be erected. If my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) objects to their being erected here, I know other places that would be glad to have them. In my humble opinion they ought to be at the capital. I agree with my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) and what he proposes I hope to do at an early date-to make a report showing the best locations for tliese buildings and to purchase land which will be sufficient for years to come.

The impression made upon the mind of the ordinary business man, I should think, would be that we might call a halt in this matter of a mint. It has been before us a great many years. We had expressions of opinion from very high authority, even so high as the Minister of Finance, that a mint in this country is not needed, and is, in some respects, undesirable. It would certainly cost an enormous amount of money. For the life of me, I cannot understand what advantage Canada is to get from it. I think we should get far more advantage out of the proposal of my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) of buying a large block of land at one transaction upon which buildings could be erected suitable for the purpose of government, the whole to be carried out according to some comprehensive plan. The great objection I have, not only as a member of this House, but as a business man, is to the cheese-paring way with which this thing has been gone about, not only during the last six or seven years, but during the last twenty or thirty years. When this magnificent building was put up-then was the time to have acquired an immense amount of property ; it would have been very valuable to the country now. But, having missed that opportunity, we should not go on making the same mistake year after year. I would suggest the Minister of Public AVorks to call a halt in this very matter we are discussing, and let us see if we cannot work it in with the larger scheme to the advantage of the country. I do not believe the business men of Canada have got into their minds what advantage a mint is going to be to the country. We have done and are doing a good deal for glory ; let us do something for profit and for business reasons. The city of Ottawa is of great importance we all acknowledge. But, if we are to have a mint there are other business centres in this country. This is business, not politics. There is the city of Montreal, very near us, and the city of Toronto, not very far away. Then we have Vancouver in the west, which has the advantage of being much nearer the gold producing country than Ottawa is. As to making money, we know that large amounts are being made here, and many people in the city of Ottawa are becoming enormously



wealthy. If a little daylight is let in, I think we may find that we are getting too many money making institutions in the city of Ottawa. Let the government take the country into their confidence in this matter. We find that the site looked upon as good not five months ago is now regarded as inadequate. How will the whole question be regarded ten years from now ? The government should take this matter seriously, and not go about it as if they were speculators on the stock exchange. Surely it must be a serious matter, seeing that it has occupied attention for three years. The hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) who is a good business man, does not understand what you are trying to do. Is it politics or business ? I think the time has come when we should stop driving at politics and settle down to business. The government do not seem to regard these matters seriously. The Minister of Finance particularly, in his jaunty fashion, plays battle dore and shuttle cock with these questions. But he cannot do it all the time. The country is waking up, and I think we shall wake up the government and compel them to treat public affairs seriously and not answer, as the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) did the other day when he was asked a plain business question, with a ridiculous comical story. The government are being watched from one end of the country to the other. Let them turn their eyes to the west, and they will see their friends in power in the province of Ontario being arraigned before the people. These things cannot be turned aside with a jaunty sneer. This matter of erecting a mint in Ottawa may be treated by the government as a small matter, but the country cannot be humbugged about it all the time. The Minister of Finance may meet a committee in this city and, with his cleverness, appear to turn them down. But the only effect is to send emissaries throughout the country who feel that they have not been fairly treated. And I can tell you, Mr. Chairman, that the time is coming when there will be a change.
Oh, oh.

The very laugh, the very sneer I hear from the other side emphasizes what I say. Hon. gentlemen opposite know it. There is not a man coming from a constituency in Ontario who does not know this, and there is not one of their supporters from Ontario who does not tell them of it. They are trying to withstand a movement that has been helped on by the action of the late Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) who honestly tried to voice what is the real feeling of the country and what would bel best in the interest of the country. The Minister of Finance, I claim, is turning this thing down, and he is turning it down to the detriment of his friends and the party to which he belongs. I am not

here to make an excuse for the hon. gentlemen opposite, I will be glad to see them turned down. Now, Sir, I submit that a matter of this kind, although it appears to be small, is really of great importance, as showing the trend of opinion in this country. It is significant that a matter can be brought up here year after year for three, years, and that the whole country can be misled, moreover, that the very city in which this building is supposed to be built can be misled. I think we are justified in concluding that the government have not been honest in this matter, and that they are now endeavouring to hoodwink the people of this country in connection with this mint.

I must defend what I have done in the past. I think I am on fair ground in saying that the government, while I was a member of it, did not purposely lose any time. As I said, the plans had to be prepared here first, and then they had to be approved on the other side. That took time. But tenders were asked for before I left, and were received, and if there had been no change in the site the work would be going on now.
The change of the minister was the principal thing.

Now it may be well that the committee should realize thoroughly what that royal mint means. We have been discussing it in the past. I, for one, would have been glad to have a Canadian mint, but after discussion it was found that perhaps that would not be practicable. It was resolved to have a branch of the royal mint, which means of course that the superior officers of the institution will not be Canadians but Englishmen, the imperial government will appoint them. Practically this institution would not be under our care and control.
Do the imperial government pay anything towards it ?
No.
Oh, Canada pays the bill.

On that question as on all others, my motto is Canada for the Canadians. But I fully realize that it would not be practicable or possible to have a purely Canadian mint. The idea of the Minister of Finance was to have a royal mint so that we might work for the imperial government. But on the other hand, we would have to pay for the institution though it would not be under our care and charge. That is about the size of it, and it is just as well that we should look the matter straight in the face. The government have decided on that policy, and I am equally responsible for it. But as the government have not moved in the matter, it is just as well perhaps that we pause over

the position as we find it to-day. I must give the Minister of Finance this credit, that he has always been anxious for the work to proceed, and it is not his fault if the work has not progressed more rapidly'. We pushed the plans in England as quickly as we could. Of course if we are obliged to buy a new site, it will cost a large amount of money. Land is not given free in this capital of ours. If the original site has been condemned-well, later on when the proper time comes, I shall desire to know the reasons why it has been condemned. I went carefully over the ground again and again with the chief architect, as well as with other able men,, and we thought that [DOT] the site was a very proper one indeed, otherwise I would not have consented to it.

The Minister of Public Works made one or two remarks which I think are a little unkind, and he attributed opinions to me which I do not hold. He said that the member for Ottawa (Mr. Bir-kett) did not wish to have the mint built in this city, that there were plenty of other places anxious to get it. Now the member for Ottawa did not say one word against putting up any building in Ottawa, but he did ask why the building had been abandoned, and why, after this vote had been repeatedly taken, nothing was done. Surely I would be the last man in this House to say a word against one dollar being spent in Ottawa. I want to see all the money possible spent in this city, and I do not like to have any one insinuate that I am not anxious to see that building go on. The fact is that I see no reason why it has not been gone on with. The vote was taken three years ago, the plans are prepared, the site chosen is excellent. I do not see why the site should be changed, and in my opinion there is no reason for any change.

Of course I only spoke in a jocular manner. The hon. gentleman referred to the vote off $200,000, he was mistaken in that, for I looked back three years and found the same vote, $50,000. I myself am in favour of building the mint in Ottawa, and sincerely desire to see the work go on as quickly as possible. There is no intention on the parti of the government of delaying it any longer than is necessary.
That is perfectly satisfactory.
Could the ministei* say whether a proclamation has been issued by the imperial authorities establishing a branch of the royal mint in Ottawa ?

I cannot say as to the issue of the proclamation, but arrangements have been made between the imperial and Canadian governments for the establishment of a royal mint. Whether the proclamation has been actually 12i
issued I do not remember at the moment; but I am clear in stating that all the arrangements have been made between the two governments to authorize the establishment of a mint at Ottawa, in accordance with the Act passed unanimously by this House.
The Act was predicated upon proclamation issued by the imperial authorities and published in the Canadian ' Gazette,' establishing a branch of the royajl mint at Ottawa.

I do not think that would prevent our going ahead. I am not sure the proclamation has been issued, I almost think it has not, but it would be issued the moment the mint has been established and put in operation. However, there is no misunderstanding, there is perfect agreement between the imperial and the Canadian governments, and the correspondence on the subject was brought down at a previous session.
When does the hon. gentleman think this mint will be established and in running order ?
The Minister of Public Works can best answer that
I mean the other arrangements after the building is erected.
Just as soon as the building can be erected.

Instead of regretting the delay that has occurred, I think it is rather fortunate that delay has*occurred. I think a good deal could be said about this, and a great deal of thinking could be done about it. Now, we have had a great deal of discussion as to the question of the necessary public buildings at Ottawa and as to the sites for them and it surely does occur to the government, as it has occurred to many hon. members, that we do not want one public building in one part of the city and another public building in another part and thus have them distributed around through the city of Ottawa. There ought to be some definite and complete plan as to where the public buildings which are likely to be required in the next half century will be located. Now, we are met with the difficulty at the present time that there is no site for this building, and that because- and it may be a very good reason-it is contemplated by the government that they may have to purchase some private property, it is not expedient at the present time to take the committee into their confidence and tell them where that site is to be. That, I can understand is perfectly reasonable, but, at the same time, I think it is probably a good reason why this item should not be pressed at the present time. I do not think- and in this I differ from a great many hon.

members who have spoken-that there is any great urgency in regard to this matter. If I understand the hon. Minister of Public Works aright, he suggested, during an early part of the discussion, that probably he would have a report from his chief engineer to-morrow. Was I right ?
No, within a few days.

I thought he said to-morrow; however, within a few days. I know I cannot prevail very far upon the government and probably as a new member my views are not entitled to any great weight, but I would suggest that in view of the fact that we are liable to have this report in a few days and as there is no great urgency in passing this item at the present time, it be allowed to stand over, if it meets with the concurrence of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, and that we take it up again when we have more information than we have at the present time.

Let me say that I must insist upon pressing this vote if we are to make any progress at all. This matter has been before the House for three years at least, and I think it was unanimously admitted by both sides of the House that it was in the interests of the country that this work should go on. Perhaps, unexpected circumstances have arisen to create some delay, but it is better to have some delay than to make a mistake. If the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) understood the conditions at all he would see that this building should under no circumstances be put in a situation near the other buildings used for parliamentary or public purposes. You would not want a factory with a wall around it like a gaol placed in the beautiful park around this building for instance. We should have our geological museum and such other national buildings as we require near each other if we could get a plot of land under reasonable conditions that would answer for some years. At the same time, no one would think of establishing this manufacturing industry on the same ground as that occupied by the class of buildings to which I have referred.
It must be isolated.
I think that when the supplementary estimates are brought down, I shall be prepared with full information upon this subject.
On this subject ?
On this subject.
If the money is voted it is to be expended on a building in Ottawa ?
Yes.

It is stated that this amount has been voted three times without any objection. The hon. gentleman must know that he is asking this vote under entirely different conditions from those that formerly prevailed. It was voted the last time on the express condition that the site which had been selected was to cost nothing. Now the hon. gentleman comes down and asks for this vote without being prepared to tell the Committee, and the Committee has not insisted on knowing, what the building would cost, but, surely, the hon. gentleman will not expect the Committee to vote a sum of money blindly when, it can be delayed for a few days and when the Committee does not know how much will be involved in securing a suitable site, information on which point may change the minds of the Committee entirely as to whether we should undertake that work or not.
I uuderstand that work to be one more of rational pride than of absolute utility or necessity for Canada. The first impulse that seized the House was that we should have a Canadian mint, not because we absolutely needed it but from a sense of national pride. We have been forced to abandon that position and to take another position. Now, so far as the benefits accruing to Canada from the standpoint of dollars and cents are concerned, we have not even from the hon. Minister of Finance any encouragement to hope that our position will be materially changed. We are told that if we had a Canadian mint it would not be in operation for more than one month in the year, but what assurance have we, when we are taking another mint upon ourselves and investing so large a sum of money-and it is a British mint, not a Canadian mint, separately as was understood in the first instance-of the necessity that has arisen under which we should give the hon. gentleman this vote until we see the question somewhat worked out ? I think the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) is quite proper in suggesting that Canada can live without a branch of the imperial mint for another year. Now, the question is that if there is one established in Canada, will it be in Ottawa ? That seems to be a settled question, and I think the hon. gentleman can well afford to allow that vote to stand. We do not know what complications will arise in connection with the new site that may /change the mind of parliament entirely, because the hon. gentleman is asking the vote under new conditions.

Just a word, Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. minister in regard to my not appreciating the point that this building, possibly being surrounded by a wall, or probably surrounded to some extent by a substantial iron railing, or paling, should not be in close association with the buildings here. I quite apprehend that

point, but the point I wish to make clear is that there should be some relation of the public buildings, one to the other, that it is not desirable that we should have certain public buildings here and the mint in an entirely different part of the city, unconnected as a matter of view, even, with the present location. I have too much of an eye for architectural beauty and the fitness of things to desire to see it even in the place where it was proposed, at one time, to erect a statue to our late sovereign the Queen-at the entrance to the public buildings here. I do not propose that it should be upon this plot of ground at all, but I do consider that when we were discussing the question before that it was pretty well understood a site had been fixed upon, and that while it was an isolated site in every way appearing to be suitable, was well within the view of the public buildings we have here and was to form part of a group of buildings proposed to be erected at a considerable cost. I say again, and I say it much more urgently than before, that I think it is not only the courtesy we should expect from the hon. minister that he should allow the matter to stand over, but it is the right of the representatives of the people, having regard to the changed conditions that have arisen, to ask that this item shall not be pressed at the present time. Let me be as distinct and definite as possible. X want to say here that having regard to the changed conditions I shall feel it to be my duty, at all events, to protest in the most vigorous way by vote, or otherwise, against this matter being pressed whilst the people's representatives are not in a position to know where the building is to be placed.

We are not discussing, or we should not be discussing, to-night, the wisdom or unwisdom of establishing a Canadian mint. After several years of discussion on this subject the parliament of Canada came to the conclusion unanimously that it was a wise measure to have ; not a Canadian mint as was originally proposed, but a branch of the royal mint. I stated to my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) that if he had read that interesting speech of 1899 carefully he would have observed that at the very time at which I dissented from the motion then made respecting the establishment of a purely Canadian mint-in that very speech I suggested that if an arrangement could be made with Her Majesty's government for establishing a branch of the royal mint, that would give larger employment than a purely Canadian mint, that would probably be a very desirable arrangement. That arrangement which I then suggested was afterwards carried out. This was fully understood when parliament unanimously adopted that Act, and my hon. friend the leader of the opposition was one of its most cordial supporters. Therefore, we are not discussing to-day the
wisdom of establishing a branch of the royal mint in Canada. I admit it was to some extent a matter of national pride, but national pride is not less to-day than it was two years ago. If we are open to complaint at all it is not because we have adopted the policy of building a branch of the royal mint, but because there has been some delay. I see no reason in the world why we should not proceed with this vote so that if there has been delay in the past there shall not be delay in the future. We have unanimously adopted the policy of having a mint, my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Brock) voted in support of it and he must not go back upon himself. I want him to be consistent. I want him to stand to his guns ; he supported the royal mint here only a few years ago for national and imperial reasons, and I do not want him to be less national and less imperial than at that time. I think I am correct in stating that when the proposal was made to establish a mint the question of the site was not then considered essential.
Yes it was.

I will not contradict my hon. friend, because he may have looked it up and I have not; we can see about that later. I do not think the question of site was at first considered essential, but it came up later. Without stating now where the site is to be, I am quite satisfied that the cost of the land will not materially change the situation. I can not go further than that. I can assure my hon. friend who has raised a doubt on that point, that from what I know as to the progress that has been made in getting a site, the cost of that site will not be a reason for changing our policy respecting the mint.

I stand up Mr. Chairman, again to justify myself. The Finance Minister has charged that when this mint was proposed I strongly favoured it. I strongly favour everything still that tends to imperial interests as well as Canadian interests, but even suppose I have changed my opinions in regard to this matter I can say as the Prime Minister said the other day that I have been green in my youth and that I have a right to change my opinion. But let me say, Sir, that I have not changed my opinion. I agree with the opinion of the Bank of Montreal, that it is a bad business, that it will be a losing business, that there is no profit in it, and if I led the majority of this House to carry me with it I simply did what the Finance Minister did himself.
Let us stand together then.

I contend that the establishment of a mint in this country will redound to the financial loss of this country, and if that be the case, it is not beneath the dignity of the Minister of Finance to recede from his mistake when he finds he has made one.

I do not see wliy I should drag Canada into a serious loss of $100,000 a year merely for the sake of national pride. We can distribute our national pride much more profitably in another direction. We can assist our great empire to which we belong much more liberally than we are doing at present, we can spend our money much more profitably than by spending it on a mint which the Finance Minister is going to take to his own particular glory instead of the national glory of this country. So far as my opinion goes, now I advise the members of this House to move very slowly in this matter. It is not merely the expenditure on the building that we have to consider.

How much will it cost
a year ?
The Act of Parliament provides for.an annual expenditure of $75,000.

But the Minister of Finance told us that he was making a profit by having the silver coined in England instead of here, and to that $75,000 you must add the loss which we incur in that regard. But you forget the patronage there is in connection with such a department. Why bless your heart they can keep Ottawa solidly Reform for years to come with the patronage they vyill have.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Oh.

I would ask the members of this House to be very careful about adopting the financial schemes of the Finance Minister. He will allow his financial ability to be directed in any way that will keep him where he is. This country knows it; we have all recognized it. It has been impressed upon me personally ; it has been impressed on this side of the House and I think the members on the other side of the House are impressed too. Therefore, I would ask gentlemen who have an interest in this country, and I think we all have, I would ask them to vote down this scheme even supposing we go back on our record. We have the advantage of the opinion of the First Minister that it is justifiable under certain circumstances to go back upon our record. I am not ashamed of changing my opinions if I change them in the right direction, and the right direction at the present time is to sit upon an expenditure of this kind. We are floating upon the crest of that wave of prosperity which the Finance Minister spoke of some years ago. He knows as well as any man in this House, and the sensible level headed business men of this country are warning him every day that we are approaching a time when things will not be as prosperous. We are not only putting up a mint now, but we are putting up a building in which we are going to carry on a very losing business. There is no need for it at all ; there is not a bit of glory in it; we are perfectly satisfied Mr. BROCK.
with our present currency and the manner in which our coinage is at present turned out. Gentlemen I ask you to oppose this Canadian mint in every possible way, and I do ask the Finance Minister to have the grace, once in his life, to acknowledge that he has been possibly wrong and to let this thing drop.
I have no objection to admit that I may be possibly wrong sometimes.
And you are wrong now.

I have to disagree from the hou. member (Mr. Brock) with regard to this expenditure. He objects to it because the expenditure may be directed in such a way as to keep the present government in power for many years. Thank goodness, the application of the money is not in their hands at all. It has to be paid direct to the Lord Commissioners of the Treasury in England.
What becomes of the patronage story ?
It is the patronage part of my hon. friend's argument that I object to.
They will fix that.

Even the officers are to be appointed by the imperial authorities. The Act provides for an annual expenditure of $75,000 to be paid into the hands of the Lord Commissioners of the Treasury in order to meet the salaries and contingencies of that department. My hon. friend (Mr. Brock) need have no fear that it will be expended so as to injure any political party. I am with the hon. gentleman opposite that the mint should be erected in Ottawa. But I do not know that it will be a great success financially, or that a large amount of money will accrue to the country because of it. I heard the objection of Mr. Clouston. of the Bank of Montreal, as to the establishment of the mint, but I think it was predicated on the establishment of a Canadian mint. Under the new circumstances, I do not know whether there will be a profit or a loss ; but I think there will be no great loss of money, after all, in the establishment of this institution, as we have the assurance of the hon. Minister of Public Works that it will be built in Ottawa, and that after the building is completed the expenditure, in the shape of patronage, in the appointments to the different offices in the mint, will be in hands that will not exert a corrupt influence on the electors of Ottawa.

Notwithstanding all that has been said, I beg to move that the item be struck out. In doing that, we shall be on the safe side for Canada, at any rate.
Amendment negatived :	Yeas, 6 ; nays,
47.

Victoria Memorial Museum, $50,000.

This is a revote, as the House knows. My own personal view is to recommend council to purchase a block of land that will be sufficient ; and before I ask for any money to go on with this building, that will be reported to the House.
In other words, no site has been chosen as yet.
No.

I want to call the attention of the hon. gentleman to the necessity of a new press gallery in this chamber. The press gallery is crowded, and the press boys would like to have some more accommodation. If my hon. friend will kindly give his attention to my request, I shall be very much obliged indeed.

I may say that in view of the improvement which was made last year, giving so much satisfaction to members of the House, I think it will be proper to ask for a supplementary estimate to continue that improvement on the other side, and I will ask the architect to report what accommodation can be given to the press gallery.

I think it is the unanimous opinion of the members of this House that the construction of a national museum is of the very greatest importance at the present time. I am not so much concerned about the construction of a mint; but so far as the geological museum is concerned, it seems to me that we are flirting with calamity to allow the precious records of this country to be kept in an old building which is liable at any moment to be swept away by fire, and I think the minister cannot act too quickly in securing a site and going on with the construction of a new building.

I am entirely opposed to the principle of voting a large amount of money year after year without knowing when it is to be used or whether it is to be used at all. It is a very unsound and pernicious principle, and I respectfully submit that the ministers ought to be prepared to give the House more information than they do as to whether the money is intended to be used or not. If it is not to be used we should not be asked to vote it, and if it is, then they ought to be in a position to give us some particulars about it. The hon. gentleman says the site is not yet selected. Is it intended that any portion of the vote shall be expended during the present year ?

I approve in a general way of the remarks
of my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule). In regard to this particular vote, I believe the desire of the great majority of the members of this House has been expressed by my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan), that some provision should be made for such a building as he has spoken of. Before we proceed with the work, I will bring the fullest possible information before the House, and I hope to give the full cost.

There were two or three sites in view when I left office. If I may be allowed, I would suggest to my hon. friend that he should not be cheeseparing in this matter. This is a very important building, and it should be located on a site that would do credit to this country. A few thousand dollars more or less for the purchase of a site for such a building should not be considered for a moment. I had first contemplated locating the building in the Major Hill Park, over the pond there ; but on reflection, and after having consulted some of my colleagues, I made up my mind that that would not do. I had another site in view, a very fine site indeed, and one which I thought would not be too expensive. It would not be in the public interest to say where it is.
Would it be convenient to the buildings ?

In all the big-capitals of the world the public buildings are not together. It is out of the question to suppose that we can locate all our buildings in the same locality. It seems to me that a building of this kind should have an ornamental site, and I do not think the House will object to the purchase of a fine site, even if the price is a little high.

I do not wish to be understood as opposing the expenditure. I am opposing the principle of asking the House to spend money without knowing what we are committing ourselves to. The hon. minister says that if we vote this item he will give us the information later. But, if we should object afterwards to vote any more money, we will be met with the statement that we had committed ourselves to this expenditure long ago.

My intention is to bring down all the details, and we will let the item stand.
Some resolutions reported.
